title: Magnesium-Assisted Combustion Synthesis of TiC Nanoparticles
content: Titanium carbide (TiC) is a refractory compound characterized by a high melting point of 3260 K and a microhardness of 30.4 GPa. It is primarily used as an abrasive and as a reinforcing agent for aluminum alloys [1]. Due to these properties, TiC is attractive for applications in the automotive and aerospace industries, which demand lighter materials with greater strength. To synthesize TiC, titanium (Ti) powders must be combined with a carbon (C) source, such as graphite, graphene, or multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) [2]. A technique that has recently gained attention for TiC synthesis is magnesiothermy. In particular, the magnesiothermic reduction process is a traditional-yet-effective high-temperature, self-propagating synthesis (SHS) method [3]. The motivation for this work is to synthesize in situ TiC composites. Mixtures of 0.9 g of titanium powder (Alfa Aesar, 99,5 %), 0.1 g of carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs), and hydrochloric acid (J. T. Baker, 36.5%) were prepared in accordance with methods reported in the literature [4]. Subsequently, the powders were homogenized in an agate mortar for 30 minutes. Pellets were then formed at a compaction pressure of 218 MPa [5]. The sample was coated with 3 g of metallic magnesium wafers (Superior, 99%) to initiate ignition. This step was carried out under a CO2 atmosphere to prevent reactions with atmospheric oxygen. Structural characterization was carried out via X-ray diffraction (XRD) using a Panalytical X’pert PRO diffractometer, operated at 40 kV and 30 mA with CuKα radiation (λ = 0.15406 nm) in Bragg–Brentano geometry. Scanning electron microscopy coupled with energy dispersive spectroscopy (SEM-EDS, HITACHI SU3500) at 30 kV was employed to examine both morphology and elemental composition. The microstructure of TiC was further examined via high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HR-TEM, JEOL JEM2200FS) operating at 200 kV. Selected area electron diffraction (SAED) was also performed to complement the structural analysis. XRD pattern indexation with Match! software (01-089-3828 ICSD) confirmed that the TiC structure is isostructural with halite, exhibiting a cubic phase and space group Fm-3m (No.225). An average crystallite size of 24.3 nm was determined by applying the Scherrer equation with instrumental correction. In the SEM micrograph (Fig. 1(a)), TiC particles are observed arranged in randomly assembled layers, while Fig. 1(b) illustrates the orientation of these compacted layers (blue arrow). Previous authors suggest that compacting the Ti and C powders to form the pellet leads to the formation of a magnesium wafer coating, which in turn promotes the formation of these layers. Due to the abrupt temperature increase during synthesis, a portion of the material (MWCNTs, marked with red arrows) remains unreacted. Figure 2(a) shows a SEM image of the area subjected to elemental mapping via EDS, while Figure 2(b) displays the results confirming the presence and distribution of Ti/ C in that region. Figure 3(a) presents an HR-TEM image where a circled area reveals both a segment of a nanotube and the formation of TiC. The CrysTbox software, in combination with the CIF file, was used to index the diffraction rings observed in the SAED pattern (see Figure 3(b)). This result is consistent with the XRD analysis for TiC [6].
